utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, will you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm Lieutenant Harry Konings. I'm a member of the Royal Netherlands Army and my current job is staff officer, land operations, in the Land Forces Doctrine and Training Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe your background both in your present military as well as your position with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My general background in the Royal Netherlands Army is being an artillery officer. My first functions in the Netherlands army was in artillery units, battery commander, battery officer, operations officer of an artillery battalion. I have had various functions in staffs, here in The Hague and in other areas in the Netherlands. And my experience in United Nations is that I have been a United Nations military observer from the end of April 1995 until the end of October 1995, and during that period I was stationed in Sarajevo, and I have some other experiences on the Balkan being a EU observer in Croatia and an OSCE observer in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Prior to today were you given an opportunity to review your transcript of your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, which bears the 65 ter numbers 9453 for 12 March 2007, and 9454, for 13 March 2007?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If asked those same questions today would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My answers will be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May that please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Pursuant to Rule 92 ter, I tender 65 ter 2797, previously admitted -- or previously addressed in the Dragomir Milosevic case, as P85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 8607, previously P361, admitted at transcript 36 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I apologise. Certainly. I tender 65 ter 8607, previously admitted as P361, admitted at transcript 3610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And finally, 65 ter 8608, previously admitted as P362, at transcript page 3610 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I now turn to the present evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Konings in the Dragomir Milosevic case you were shown a series of five photographs and were required to annotate two. For clarity of the record, we must undergo this exercise again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I call up 65 ter 8606.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, at page 3605 of your Dragomir Milosevic transcript you identified features of this photograph which later became P358 in that case. With the assistance of the usher I would like to have you mark a few items on this photograph. Can you please circle the "famous library" and mark it with an A.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court why is that library famous?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, it's one of the famous buildings inside the city of Sarajevo with quite some history and in the war it was -- it was completely burned, and for that reason it was he a very significant landmark. And for us as UNMOs, especially working on the observation post from where this picture is taken, it was a -- let's say, it was a landmark that we could use for recognising other parts in the city, because it is very significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the land -- observation post from where you took this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This observation post was called OP-1, and it was an observation post belonging to the team, the UNMO team that I was a member of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Where in Sarajevo is it situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The observation post is -- was situated in the mountains at the south side of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which mountains specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which mountain specifically, if you do know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It were -- well, I could point it out on the map. I don't recall the specific name. I think it was called Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I will finish with this photograph and then I'll actually undergo the exercise to identify where OP-1 was actually located.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher can I again have you circle the area in which your team base was located and mark with a B?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The area was -- I have to do it very roughly because the picture is not so clear. The area the team base was located is in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your team base called?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In the first days that I came there the team base was called Sierra Charlie 1, which stands for Sarajevo Central 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in UNMO documents how would Sierra Charlie one be designated? Is there an acronym for that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, we used the term Sierra Charlie 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For non-military personnel, if we see it written will it be SC-1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It will be SC-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask that this photograph can have a screen shot and it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As the Court had asked where your observation post was actually located, I would like to undergo the exercise of explaining how one locates certain positions on the map of Sarajevo. To the left of you is a full-size map which has been previously admitted in this case as P439 as part of the map book itself. Given that this is going to be a larger indication I would like your assistance. Can you please describe for the Court using grid lines how one located certain positions on an UNPROFOR map.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Using grid lines is not specifically limited to UNPROFOR maps. It is generic military system used throughout armed forces in the world. On a military map, you will find a system of squares, which are visible here on the map. The blue lines forms squares. And every square is one by one kilometre, and all the squares have numbers. I have to bend towards the map in order to see. For example, this one, this line has the number 94, which brings the next line to 93, there is a logical system which counts from west to east. The other lines are numbered 56, 57, 58 running from bottom to top. Once you want to designate a location, you first start with the vertical line and then you name the horizontal line. So, for example, if you want to have a location that is in the grid square 9456, you say -- you take first that grid, you say 9456. But within a square you can be more precise. You can divide that square which is one by one kilometre. You can decide the vertical line and the horizontal line in pieces equal pieces of, for example, 100 metres which brings you a much more precise location. So once you read 941, 561 that gives you a location on 100 metres precise. What you do then is you take first the vertical line 94 and from 94 you go 100 metres to the right, then you take 56, and you go 100 metres up, which brings you on the precise position on that grid square. You even can do it more precise up to ten metres. Then you say 9411, 5611, which brings you on a location that has an accuracy of ten metres. And in certain circumstances, but that was never done in Sarajevo but in certain other military situations you need to have even an accuracy of one metre, which gives you a grid reference of ten ciphers, for example, 96111, 56111, which brings you an accuracy on one metre exactly. For example, when you want to designate the exact point of a road junction, the middle of a road junction, it might be necessary in certain circumstances that you designate that absolutely within one metre. But under normal circumstances, you have enough for ten metres, or as we did in UNPROFOR, we never went further than 100 metres because that was for our purposes was enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At this time I would like to focus on a small block of the map that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would ask that we pull up 65 ter 2719 to be brought up at document ID 0361-5780-1. That will bear a 65 ter actually of 021 -- I'm sorry, 02719.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't been transcribed, Madam Carter, for the last sentence that you said. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. I said that the 65 ter is actually 0217 -- I'm sorry. My eyesight is not that good. 02719.01 and the image is now before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the image before you is this in fact a portion of the larger map you were just speaking of?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a portion reflecting the central old part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On this map, are you able to locate the location of OP-1? And with specificity, in the daily sitreps that have been admitted into this case, we have indication that that location is actually at BP 940586.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You have now made a triangle over a portion of the map. Are you indicating that that is the location of OP-1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, a triangle with -- I tried to make a dot in there, but a triangle with a dot refers to the -- that's the military symbol for an observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you can also put to the right of that, OP-1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask that a screen shot be taken of this image and it is tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, from Observation Post 1 we did see the photograph of what was visible from there but can you describe the general areas. What neighbourhoods or portions of Sarajevo were visible from your observation post?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, actually from that observation post, my team could view practically the whole area of operations that was designated to team SC-1. And the most important area to that was the central old part of the city, which you can see here on the map in the dark -- darker brown colour along the river. But everything up to the north, which starts to be in yellow above the words Stari Grad, which is in the central part of the map, was also belonging to the area of operations and was also visible from the OP-1. Also visible from OP-1 were the confrontation lines north of the area of operations. So the view we had from there, given of course weather circumstances, was very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the photograph that we actually just saw, what type of camera did you use in order to catch that type of view from OP-1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It was a very small private analogue camera, not digital or anything, which fitted in the -- in one of the pockets of my uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So the image that we were able to see, that is pretty much the image you were able to see on site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would now ask that -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would actually ask to call up 65 ter 8604 and we will be making additional markings on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in your Dragomir Milosevic transcript at 3608, you were asked to circle the twin towers on this photograph, which became an annotated photograph, P360, in that case. Can you, with the assistance of the usher, undergo the same exercise here today?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if you will mark the twin towers with an A.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At that same point in the Dragomir Milosevic transcript you were also asked about the location of Major Knustad and Major Conway on 28 August 1995 when they observed the impacts at Markale II. Can you please mark this location with a K and C?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And for clarity, there was indication in the Dragomir Milosevic case that where you have now marked that as, in fact, you on site at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. And I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one is yourself? The one with the blue beret or the other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one with the blue beret, that's myself. The other two were Danish soldiers helping up building a proper OP, because we were standing completely in the open, as you can see. So we got some help from a Danish unit, Danish UN unit in the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we understand unit, this is not the day you observed the Markale II thing. This was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... standing where the people who observed stood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if I could have this photograph screen shot and then an exhibit number given to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to turn your attention to air bombs. In your time in Sarajevo, did you ever encounter an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I, at least, can recollect two -- two times that an air bomb was used and that I did an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would call up 65 ter 8135.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And while that is being brought on screen can you please describe the investigations you performed on these two air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the testimony not being sought to be adduced, as I understand this witness's testimony, this witness is being called pursuant to 92 ter. Under the guidelines that were promulgated and specifically paragraph 21, it states that the party calling a witness under 92 ter may be permitted by the Trial Chamber to read out a short summary of the witness's statement and/or conduct a limited direct examination of the witness where such examination is focussed on clarifying or highlighting particular aspects of his statement. With regard to the issue of air bombs, no such testimony was adduced through the 92 ter statement and is therefore outside of the 92 ter offerings that are made here and would seem to be in violation of the guidelines as set forth for purposes of the conduct of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Rule 92 ter itself indicates that a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement. The Prosecution is relying upon the in part aspects of the Rule 92 ter. While we understand that the Prosecution is limited when it does submit certain aspects of a witness's testimony pursuant to 92 ter that it will not be allowed to lead evidence in full on those points but rather left be only to highlight certain aspects or to clarify other aspects. The portion in regards to air bombs we are actually tendering as live testimony as indicated in the witness's 65 ter summary where it specifically indicates that this witness will also give evidence of investigations he made on the firing of air bombs which took place on 16 June 1995. Thus, we rely on the wording of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then it is our respectful submission that this witness should have been identified as a viva voce witness and not a 92 ter witness from the very beginning. As early as the 23rd February, 2007, he listed as and identified as a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear. I thought -- when you first answered I thought you were at cross purposes with Mr. Guy-Smith, and at the end of your explanation I then thought you have answered this objection. Let me understand the objection, Mr. Guy-Smith. I thought you were saying that a 92 ter witness is restricted to giving a summary of issues that were mentioned in his previous testimony if it is his testimony that is being tendered or a report or statement. Now, are you saying that whatever it is that is -- that this witness wrote previously, does not refer to air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That therefore he is going outside the ambit of what is being tendered by way of his previous testimony or statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it your position that he didn't testify like -- what is the document that is being tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a -- the document that -- the documents that have been tendered to the Chamber by way of the 92 ter package are the -- are parts of the former testimony in the form of a transcript in the Milosevic case and the exhibits that were discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you're saying in that -- in his testimony in the Milosevic case he didn't refer to air bombs at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then, Madam Carter, it does then seem as if you are talking at cross purposes with your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- Mr. Guy-Smith appears to indicate that -- if a witness is called pursuant to Rule 92 ter, only the aspects that were addressed in that prior transcript will be allowed to be led. However, Rule 92 ter itself at Rule 92 ter (A) indicates that a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thus we are not relying on the previous transcript of the witness in relation to air bombs but rather leading that evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But let's understand what that paragraph means. That part of the paragraph means -- that part means that can you either admitted the entire previous statement or part of it. Not that you can add to it new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that there is it jurisprudence in other Chambers before the Tribunal that indicates the opposite. That it -- the 92 ter package addresses only what is going to be coming in by that written evidence. However, it has been understood by other Chambers to mean that that means you can also call other aspects live. For example, in the Milutinovic Chamber we were held by that same rule. If it the indication of this Court that they do not follow that interpretation of 92 ter, I will abide by the Court's rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not the interpretation of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I may have one brief moment to restructure my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, I will now move to your investigation of a shelling which took place on 28 August 1995, involving three little girls. At Dragomir Milosevic transcript 3603, you indicate that a 128-millimetre rocket hit a flat apartment block killing a four-year-old child and injuring two others.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to call up 65 ter 1465.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: While that is being called up, if can you please describe for the Court your investigation that took place involving these three little girls.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That investigation took place along the same lines as we did every investigation, which, briefly, was initiated after a phone call from the Sarajevo police forces, and once we had permission from our HQ, from our UNMO HQ, we went over to the scene with an UNMO team, most times consisting of two or three UNMOs, including an interpreter, and on the spot we met a police team and together we investigated. In this particular investigation, we went to the location and we found parts of the 128-millimetre rocket. We found a -- the impact place, and we also saw some human body parts of one of the children. After that, we went to the morgue in one of the hospitals, and we identified the girl. She was lying at the entrance of the morgue and we identified her being the young girl that was killed before. After that, we went to the hospital, inside the hospital, and we had a brief talk with the doctor that treated the other two girls and we had a brief meeting. We briefly saw the two girls that were taken care of. And after that, of course, we filed our report which was a necessary thing to do, and we filed that report and we sent that report to our UNMO HQ in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Prior to today's date, have you had the opportunity to review this Bosnian report on the same incident?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Does this investigate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not quite sure what you mean by "Bosnian report."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report that we see before us is not the UNMO report but rather the corresponding Bosnian report on the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "Bosnian report," you mean report by the army of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: By the police department of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The police of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think put it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review the report done by the joint investigation or the -- I'm sorry, the corresponding investigation by the Bosnian police into this incident?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have seen that report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Does the investigation report and its findings correspond with the investigation you personally performed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponds, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in fact if we move to page 3 of the document in English and page 2 in B/C/S, your name is actually specifically mentioned at number 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is -- that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you indicate to the Court that you did not work in conjunction with the Bosnian police. However, you did have parallel investigations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we did parallel investigations but we always took independent data. So we never took data that were brought in by the Bosnian police. We always relied on our own data even in cases that they -- that the data were different which happened. We kept our own data. We never gave our information to the Bosnian police because that was had -- that were the strict orders from the UNMO HQ to guard our impartiality in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, you've indicated that in relation to this specific investigation were your findings as an UNMO officer the same as the findings that were made by the Bosnian officers?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In this particular case, our findings were the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to discuss Markale II. When was the first time you saw the Markale market on 28 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: First time must have been somewhere in the morning around 9.00 or 8.30, I'm not quite sure about the exact time anymore, when I came across the Markale market on my way to the UNMO HQ, where I had a daily meeting with the Senior Military Observer and the other team leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you passed by Markale market that morning, can you please describe for the Court in detail what the market appeared like?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection; asked and answered. The information is contained in the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information is briefly touched upon within the package. I'm asking for more detail from the witness. And so I would ask to be able to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the purpose is to -- is not to expand on the evidence but to give a summary of what is already in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the guidelines of this Court indicate - and let me find the Rule - that we are allowed to expand upon -- thank you. That we are allowed to conduct a limited direct examination of the witness where such an examination is focussed on clarifying or highlighting particular aspects of the statement. What we are trying to do is to clarify and to highlight those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not expand, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Clarifying or highlighting is one thing completely distinct from expanding and leading new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I -- in when we are discussing what we are intending to do is to clarify specifically what the scene was like that morning. In detail what -- you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The idea is to clarify the evidence, ma'am. To clarify the evidence that's already been tendered. Not to give new evidence on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I may discuss with co-counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Court has indicated in relation to this evidence I will not go any further on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you did speak extensively in the Dragomir Milosevic testimony about the shelling itself and your investigation thereof. I would like to focus on a few specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would call up -- it was 65 ter 2797. Unfortunately, I don't have the exhibit number now before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that's 2292.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would call up P2292.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the item in front of you, is that the report that you drafted on the day of Markale II?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to move to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You touched, in your previous testimony, on the fact that there were actually five shells that landed on and near Markale II on 28 August 1995. I would like to address those a bit. If you can please describe for the Court or inform us, the chart that we're looking at before us, what -- what does that mean? We've got time stamps, we've got certain bearings, grid markings. Can you please describe what are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could be made visible, please. It is hardly readable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This form was a standard form issued by the UNMO organisation in UNPROFOR, in order to provide data on crater analysis. And when you start on the left-hand side, and I will take as an example the bottom -- the top line, it gives you the first line called line Alpha or A, gives you the time of the investigation, 281145 says 28 of August, quarter to 12.00 in the morning. Time B gives you time of the incident that occurred, which is 28 of August, 1114, quarter past 11.00. Line 3 gives you the grid so the location of the police of the incident. Line 3 is the bearing which gives you direction that was taken from the place of the incident to the origin of, in this case, the -- where the mortar projectile came from. That means that the direction was 170 degrees, and since that direction was taken that bearing was taken with a magnetic compass, there might be a difference between plus or minus 5 degrees. Then is stated in line 5 the type of weapon used, in this case 120-millimetre mortar, including the markings that were found on the tail of the projectile. Line 6 says whether there were fragments, shrapnels were found, yes or no; in this case, yes. Number of impacts, there was one impact. Casualties, 33 dead, 79 injured. And other damage, which in this case was superficial damage was to the main market buildings, and some extra remarks that were mentioned there in case they were applicable. And you see in this case, there were some extra remarks made as a result of the investigation we did on the spot. And in the last line, line number 11, you find the names of the patrol team of the UNMOs that did the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I would like to move back to P22 - I'm sorry - 98, the map in which you marked the observation post. Sir, on this map, with the assistance of the usher, I would like you to mark where each of these shells landed. We're going from the first in time to the last in time. If you can please mark where the two shells landed at 10.50 in the morning. The grid reference on the item we just saw indicated that one landed at 927590 --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: 92 and?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it 10.50 that it landed or 11.15 or 11.14?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, two shells hit at 10.50, two shells hit at 11.00 and the final shell on the Markale market hit at 11.14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you replete the grid, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. Based on that crater analysis you indicated that the first shell landed at 927590. And if you can mark it with a 1.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. The second shell landed at the same time at 927591.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The third shell landed at 11.00, at 928591.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The fourth shell landed at the same time at the same location. If you can mark that with a 4.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And finally, the shot that hit the Markale market landed at 11.14, at grid reference 927594.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask that a screen shot be taken of this exhibit and it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I would now to look at map P647. Just for future reference, the map before you purports to be an UNPROFOR map with grid lines as well. Would one be able to locate objects on this map in the same way that you previously did on the map ...

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, you can locate objects on this map in the same way because it is the same system of grid references.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. After 28 August, did you have any other meetings relating to Markale II?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: On the 28th and the 29th of August, I had several meetings concerning the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I call up 65 ter 2798.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What is this item?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This document is a handwritten report by myself of a meeting that I had on the 29th, a long meeting, with the investigation team, consisting of various representatives of the Bosnian authorities from the -- the high court in Sarajevo, from the police, and military experts who were trying to establish a report and an opinion what happened on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to move to page 2 of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can we clarify at this point, sir, I thought you said a little earlier that you kept strict lines between the two of you, because you wanted to maintain an impartially. From that, I got the impression that you didn't exchange notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't exchange notes, Your Honour, because this report is not given to -- to -- on that date, not given to the investigation team. What I did do is, in order of my Senior Military Observer, take part on the 28th and the 29th in the work of the investigation team of the Bosnian authorities. But we kept strictly apart and I only was there as a kind of observer, not taking part on any discussion that was made. So there were separate reports. There was a report of the Bosnian investigation team; and there was our own report that was made on the 28th; and added to that, was this patrol report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And at this meeting on the 29th, where you are meeting some authorities of the -- of Bosnia, amongst them are police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Amongst them were police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we to understand that at that stage your report had been written and immutable, couldn't be changed by any exchange of views between you and the police, and they had their own report also at that stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, now I'd like to move on to page 2 of this document. What does section 4 indicate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Section 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If can you refer us to what you are referring to on this document, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On page 2, the very first bit is saying three restrictions of movement. Number 4 is indicating meeting, and I'm just trying to illuminate what that meeting was and what the ultimate results were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move to 4. Can you please tell me is this the meeting that you're referring to, where all participants -- took place or is this something different?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. This is the report of that -- of that second meeting that took place on the 29th. Of course, a very summarised version because we were only there as observers. We did not take part of the discussion, and the meeting took place in order to finalise the Bosnian investigation that started on the 28th, and that continued on the 28th, in the evening, and continued again on the 29th, in order to write their separate report on what had happened. And the fact that we were there, again, that was in order of the UNMO HQ, even on order of the UNMO HQ in Zagreb, to be part of the -- an independent part of the investigation and the only thing we did there was listening and comparing the data that we had from the day before which were the same. We kept our data. We not -- not changed our data in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And given that this is a handwritten document that has clearly been photocopied several times, it is a bit difficult to read. If you are able, can you please read into the record what the results of that meeting were. If you're having difficulty on the screen, I do have a hard copy available for you.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, on the screen it's quite hard to read, so I would prefer to have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I can ask the assistance of the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can show that document to your opposite parties first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the part that you want me to read?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If can you read section 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It say that -- who were the participants --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could have this read verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could read it verbatim, please. I was just going to say that. Don't summarise this summary. Read it as it stands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to read, but it's very hard to read the middle part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like it says: "Participants."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Participants to the meeting to this report." I cannot read. Main --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That word is in parenthesis including -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Including Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, yes. "The aim of the meeting was to compare the reports made by UNMO patrol and the rest of the investigation team, representatives of various Bosnian authorities. Following aspects were not mentioned in the first report and can be mentioned as UNMO confirmed. In the" -- that's very hard to read. "In the time" -- and then I can't read. And it says, "of the 4 impacts, UNMOs of India-Charlie-Zulu team working on OP-1 haven't heard the outgoing nor -- neither rounds neither from Bosnian territory, general area Bicilik [phoen]" --I cannot read that, "and Colina Kapa nor from Bosnian Serb army territory. The minimum angle of impact of the 120-millimetre mortar projectile which hit the marketplace, grid 927594, was 76 degrees."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6 -- sorry. 67 degrees. 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The patrol received a list of killed and injured people, 35 killed and 78 wounded, which is added as an annex to the patrol report. See also patrol leader's remarks."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you indicated that the UNMOs were now able to confirm certain information, who were they receiving the information from and who was confirming it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Could you be a bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. When you started reading number 2 or bullet point number 2, you indicated that the UNMOs were now confirming certain information. Who was providing that information?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The extra information that we could confirm is that on the 28 of August, on the moment of the -- on the moment that the fire of shells -- fire of projectiles hit the specified places, there were two UNMOs on OP-1, and the fact that is stated here is that they did not hear any outgoing rounds from around their area, neither from the territory that was held by the BiH, neither from the territory that was held by the Bosnian Serb army. And that is quite valuable information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why is that valuable information, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, it at least told us that the projectile did not come, first of all, from Bosnian army -- BiH territory and that the projectile was fired with -- with great certainty from somewhere behind the mountains south of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who held the area behind those mountains?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The area behind that mountains was held by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would you have normally have expected the persons on OP-1 to have heard a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, the outgoing -- when a 120-millimetre mortar is fired, it gives a very loud sound. When that is done in your vicinity, not the direct vicinity but even a larger vicinity, you will hear that, and you will also notice a flash, or a small smoke. And especially on that morning because it was very clear, very silent, there were hardly any wind, sounds can carry very far in a mountainous area like there. For that reason, when a mortar would have been fired in -- in an area that was in their vicinity, they would have heard or seen it, especially since they were experienced UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have some clarification, if you can give us, please. If you look at on your screen at page 28, starting with lines 18 to line 24, you said: "The extra information that we could confirm is that on the 28th of August on the moment of the -- on the moment that the fire of shells -- fire of projectiles hit the specified places, there were two UNMOs on OP-1, and the fact that is stated here is that they did not hear any outgoing rounds from around their area, neither" - this is the point I wanted you to look at - "neither from the territory that was by the BiH, neither from that side was held by the Bosnian Serb army." I understand you to be saying they heard noise from neither of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if you go further down after that, you say at page 29, line 1: "Well, it at least told us that the projectile did not come, first of all, from BiH territory and that the projectile was fired with great certainty from somewhere behind the mountains south of the city." How do you make that determination if you heard nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can make that determination, Your Honour, because there were already investigating much more facts on the scene on the 28th of August. First of all, we had found a very clear crater. Secondly, we could designate a very clear bearing, a very clear direction which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. We're talking here before people moved down to go and do investigations. We're talking about when people are still hearing or not hearing anything. Now, you have just told us they heard from neither side any noise, and you have said that, in fact, the very fact that they didn't hear anything is valuable information. And you were asked why is it valuable? And that's how you explain that. You explain that is valuable because -- then you make a determination that the noise -- the projectile came from behind the mountains. But you are at this stage where, in fact, you have heard nothing. Now I just want to know how that determination is made, if nothing has been heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all respect, Your Honour, I -- such an investigation builds up and is a combination of various factors. If the only fact had been that we had not heard anything, then that would have been saying absolutely nothing. That would only have said no shelling from the Bosnian -- from the BiH side and no shelling from the Bosnian Serb side. But we cannot deny or we could not deny the fact that there were much more information gathered already before. And information, military information, once you gather that, you combine all that information together and then you have a piece of a puzzle again; and if you bring that all together, then you can come to the conclusion, and I was not the guy who makes that conclusions, then can you come to the conclusion, as has been done later in higher ranking reports, that there was only one possibility that the projectile came from the Serb side. So, I cannot isolate one fact on its own. I never value facts on their own. They are all part of the investigation took part on 28th and 29th and during those investigations, factors came in, new facts came in. The first fact that we found was the crater. The second fact that we found was the projectile tail. The third fact that we found was the -- the calculation that the minimum angle of impact was 67 degrees. The fourth fact that we found was that the direction, the bearing that the projectile came from was 170 degrees. The fifth fact that came in was the fact that my UNMOs on OP-1 did not hear any sound from either Bosnian territory or Bosnian Serb territory, which excluded the fact that it was fired from BiH territory. And all these facts together might bring you to the conclusion that because there was one simple very clear fact, Your Honour, there had landed a projectile in the streets of Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, I obviously was on the wrong page. Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just informed that we may be in time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In another four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Another four minutes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you had indicated that final conclusions were made and that was actually made in the UNPROFOR G2 report, admitted in this case as P67. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's one report where conclusions were made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And can you, please, describe for the Court who or what a G2 is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The G2 in any military organisation, or sometimes called the S2, is the intelligence officer who is responsible for gathering and analysing all the information concerning an enemy, opponent, adversaries, no matter how you call them. And what is important is he brings that analysis before his commanding officer, so that the commanding officer of an armed force can take his decisions what to do in the next period to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Finally, I would ask that P526 be brought on screen at page 37. Apologies, Your Honour. And if I could 65 ter 2798 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 2798 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, both in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony as well as your indication today, you indicate that the shell that caused the crater at Markale had fallen as opposed to what had been intimated in Dragomir Milosevic as having been a staged event. Can you please tell us, first of all, do you recognise the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What is this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the impact of the 120-millimetre mortar projectile in -- in the street before the market.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What do you -- what can we see or learn from this crater that indicates it is in fact an impact as opposed to any sort of other detonation on site?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, this is a very clear example of the impact of a 120-millimetre mortar. In fact, it is a typical mortar crater which is the outline which will be recognised by any military expert. Projectiles from -- impacts from artillery projectiles look quite differently. The impact on the street from an artillery projectile is differently and when you use other types of explosives, the shape charge or whatever you can think about, the impact will also be differently. Mortars were used quite often inside Sarajevo, so all involved personnel, and I mean UNMO -- UNMOs and UNPROFOR personnel had quite some experience in recognising craters created by a mortar. In the central part of the crater, you can also find the place where the fuse impacted on the -- on the soil and in the concrete, and that are the most specific aspects that can you see in a crater. One other thing is that on a 120-millimetre mortar used in that time, you quite often can find the projectile tail somewhere in the vicinity of the impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have been notified it may be time for the break again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed, ma'am. Sorry, are you saying something?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I will finish questioning after the break. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we were discussing the scene itself and what we can learn from the crater itself. Can you please describe for the Court, if the scene would have been staged in any sort of way, in relation to the projectile itself, what, if anything, would be different about the crater?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It would be my submission that the -- first of all, he is being asked to comment on a hypothetical. He has not been called as an expert but rather as a fact witness, and the opinion that is being sought at this point is an opinion of an expert. That's my first objection. I have a second objection on which I can also put forth at this time or wait, depending on what the position is with regard to the first objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put all your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. The second objection is that with regard to the hypothetical as is presently constituted, it is insufficient for an opinion to be drawn, because a staged, as it's put -- if the scene would have been staged it could have been in any sort of way. There are a variety of factors that go into a staging of a scene, so in the absence of knowing what other foundational basis upon which the opinion is being sought, the hypothetical as it presently stands has an insufficient foundation for the rendering of opinion independent of the fact that this gentleman has been called as a fact witness not as an expert and should not be rendering such an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, the witness is capable of giving testimony in regards to things that he knows for a fact -- his personal experience and that's all that we are asking for. As the last time, Mr. Guy-Smith gave the same objection before me myself, that we're not asking for an expert opinion. We're not asking for -- for him to extrapolate on things outside of his specific knowledge. So he is not being asked as an expert whatsoever, and based on the -- one moment. There's case law in regards to this, in regards on the Limaj case, the Chamber indicated that a reservoir of knowledge and understanding about a subject would be -- is what we're --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I apologise yet again. That what we're asking him to draw to upon is his reservoir of knowledge and understanding, not a specific expertise. That's as to the first objection. As to the second objection, I'm trying -- I believe that I did narrowly tailor the question to the projectile itself and to the crater impact itself. I'm not intending to delve any further than that because, frankly, in regards to the staging itself, I chose that word because that was the word that was selected in the Dragomir Milosevic case where the remainder of the scene was addressed; however, that specific item was not addressed. So I believe that I have narrowly tailored my question to the point that I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Starting with the second objection, I don't think you have sufficiently narrowed it, Madam Carter. And with -- in relation to the first objection, I think you can arrive at the same destination by asking the witness to tell us what was his findings on his investigations of this particular incident and then, of course, his -- whatever his findings were -- are, will exclude any other hypothetical situation. That will keep you on to the facts rather than on hypothesising.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, you have heard the advice of the Trial Chamber and I want to ask you specifically: Can you please tell me what about the crater that we see before us, what markers indicate that this is an impact crater as opposed to anything else?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, as I tried to explain before, this is a -- I -- I hate to use the word "perfect" but this is a perfect explanation of the explosion of a mortar projectile in a tarmac or concrete cover of the street. This kind of example -- such an example you could even use in training, because you will not find them better and more clear than here. The pattern is just as a -- as a mortar explodes, which is a not complete circle but it looks like an ellipse, and on two sides, which are aimed at -- to the left and the right of the central part of the projectile of the impact, you see a more widened pattern of shrapnels that hit the ground. Those two -- well, longer sides give you the angle of impact, direction that the projectile came from. The fuse funnel in the central part is also a very typical thing that can you see once an artillery or mortar projectile hits the soil. The difference with an artillery projectile is that due to the lower impact angle of an artillery projectile, the shape of the crater is differently. It is very distinctive again. If you would have used any other type of explosive here, you would have seen a different pattern, another pattern. Also around the scene of the crater, many aspects fit with the use of a larger mortar projectile, like shrapnels that can you find and that we did find, the tail that we found, the impact of shrapnels in the wall of the houses, broken windows, but of course broken windows can be caused by any explosions, that's not a proof. But I only can stress once more that the crater is such a, again, perfect example of what a mortar crater looks like, added to that the shrapnels and the tail, well, it is nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I thank you for your time and for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before you went to Sarajevo in your capacity working for UNMO, did you receive any training with regard to the duties you were to perform whilst in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I received specific training, not in a direct relation with Sarajevo but a training as a posting as an UNMO in general. That training was done in the Netherlands and, additionally, it was done in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what you understood your mandate to be?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Our mandate was to act impartially and to report all incidents that occurred along the area -- in the area that you were posted. And incidents, I mean military incidents like shelling, sniping, and breaking any agreement that was -- was applicable in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were considered to be the eyes and ears of the Security Council and the UN Secretary-General in the field?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can -- I can agree with such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have indicated that you worked - if I understood your testimony correctly - with UNPROFOR. Before you answer anything, my question is: Were you part of UNPROFOR, as far as you were concerned, or were you a distinct organisation from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I would choose the word -- the second part, a distinct organisation. UNMOs were administrative seen a part of UNPROFOR but they were strictly separate from that because they had their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that the UNMOs received in the field, did the UNMOs transfer that information to anyone in UNPROFOR on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did not. My team had only one responsibility. That is, report directly towards the Senior Military Observer inside Sarajevo and from there, all reports from the Sarajevo teams were collected and sent up to the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb, and what exactly happened there, that's not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us as you sit here today, how many different UNMO units were responsible for engaging in observations during the time that they were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Inside the city of Sarajevo we had, I think, about four or five times. I'm not quite sure anymore about the number. And outside Sarajevo and at the Bosnian Serb side, there were, again, I think four or five teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have a schedule or routine whereby the UNMO units that were within Sarajevo, four to five teams that you have mentioned, spoke with each other or conferred with each other on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we had regular team leader meetings, which were chaired by the Senior Military Observer or his deputy, and as far as I can recollect, they happened at least once a week and when was necessary, of course, we were called in on a more frequent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the regular meetings that you've referred to once a week, I take it that the purpose of those meetings was to coordinate and share information between the various units so that all units were similarly educated with regard to the situation on the ground, for example, that past week?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. It was an opportunity of the Senior Military Observer to speak to his team leaders, acting as a regular, normal military commander that we all were, and to coordinate all our activities and to share extra information concerning the past and the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the observations that were being made, and once again, for the moment I'm speaking in a general sense, I take it that apart from the issues that you have mentioned concerning shelling and sniping you also were mandated to engage in actual military observation, and by that I mean, what was occurring between the conflicting parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were also mandated to liaise between the conflicting parties. True?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was not given to the teams in the city. We had special liaison officers working on the Bosnian Serb side and on the BiH side. So that was not part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the special liaison officers, the special liaison officers relied, in part, upon information that you gave them so that they were in a position to have discussions with the conflicting parties. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were present during the team leader meetings. Not always but they tried to be there, especially the liaison officer from the Bosnian Serb side was frequently not present because he was not allowed to cross the lines quite often. But generally spoken, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were -- was contact had with the liaison officer on the Bosnian Serb side from the BiH side of UNMO by telephone or radio, so that the liaison officer on the Serb side would be in a position to have accurate information from the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't -- no, I don't know. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you, in your capacity, working I believe, it was in a sector Charlie 1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: SC-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: SC-1. Did you, in your capacity working in SC-1, ever receive information from your superior that had come from the Serbian liaison officer for purposes of being able to confirm or otherwise analyse information concerning an incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Telephonically? I ask -- only ask that simply because he has already testified to the fact that there were team leaders --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes, telephonically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Telephonically --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, telephonically. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have telephone contacts with the liaison officer on the Serb side. I met him not very often during the team leader meetings, and I can recall that he sketched, in that situation when he was present, the situation on a generic overview on the Serb side. But as you might recall, starting from June, there were no UNMOs left at the -- at the Bosnian Serb side because they were taken hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll get there. With regard to the team meetings where the team leaders were, during those meetings, did you share information with anyone in those meetings about information you had received from the Bosnian police?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we had -- during the team leader meetings we had a professional exchange of information between team leaders, and issues that we discussed, of course, there was how to cooperate with the Bosnian police forces on the guidelines of the Senior Military Observer, and we informed each other about the way each team was doing that, and what type of information we received through that cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What were the guidelines of the Senior Military Observer?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That we were allowed to work in cooperation with the Bosnian police. In fact, he ordered us to go to an investigation site after an incident to get in contact with the Bosnian police. Most times it happened vice versa that the Bosnian police phoned us. But we were only allowed in each case, in each separate case, to do that after discussion with the Senior Military Observer so that we got in each case his personal approval to work with the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Above and beyond that, one of your regular tasks was to verify all claims made by the conflicting parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Can you give an example of what you mean by "claims"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A claim would be, for example, the use of United Nations cars by one of the conflicting parties.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: While that was -- it might have been a task for UNMOs in other areas on the Balkans, but I have never had to work on such a claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Understanding that you have never had to work on such a claim, were any claims made by the Bosnian Serb forces that you became aware of that you had to verify?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, and saying that, I have to come back to my last answer, because I had to do an investigation on my own stolen cars, to find them back, because they were twice -- two or three times my cars from my team were stolen. And you might call that a claim, but we never found the cars back. To make the whole story complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm referring to claims by the conflicting parties, not of losing them --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you losing a car by virtue of being stolen by somebody in the area in which you were. With regard to claims made by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, did you have occasion to verify or investigate claims made by the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no claims made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I first said the Bosnian Serb forces, Your Honour, and now I'm giving the Bosnia and Herzegovina forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact both questions had been answered earlier because he said to you earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you stand corrected then I won't go back. I won't go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to issues concerning any confrontations, did you verify what was occurring at the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We had hardly any possibility to do that because we had a restricted movement close to the confrontation line, especially after June, when the UNMOs at the Serb side were taken hostage. At both sides there were very strong regulations that we were not allowed to come close to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Before you went to Sarajevo, did you understand that you were going to be working with UNPROFOR as a peacekeeping activity?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, that was the general thought that was teached -- that we were trained was the general background of peacekeeping, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived Sarajevo, you found that the notion of peacekeeping was in fact non-existent in the area; correct? Because there was a war going on. So there was no peace to keep.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, I think that's a long story. But I'm now entering my personal thoughts, and I'm not quite sure that this is the place that I reflect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question then. When you were being trained prior to the time that you arrived Sarajevo, were you trained in distinctions between peacekeeping and peace making with regard to what rules of engagement could occur?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We were trained in the whole range of peacekeeping, peace enforcing, peace making. And besides that, I'm a professional officer already all my life. So I have also knowledge of combat, war, et cetera. We have been trained in that all our life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the mandate that you went into Sarajevo with, would it be fair to say that you were informed that your mandate was one of peacekeeping not of peace making or peace enforcing?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- I'm not able to recollect the exact words that were spoken to us in our training in the Netherlands and in our training in Zagreb. The overall aspect, of course, in that time was to call the mission in -- the operation in Bosnia being a peacekeeping mission. But the thoughts about the peace to keep, in 1995, were very distinct, were very far away from that. As well, in the Netherlands, as well in our training in Zagreb. And we were -- we were clearly taught about the mandate that we had, which was to act impartially, to be the eyes and the ears of the international community, specify the UN, as you've said before, and to report any break and any incident that occurred inside the area that you would go to, because the training that we got in Zagreb was referring to a posting in either Croatia, either Bosnia-Herzegovina, or anywhere in the conflict. Only at the end of the training, it was a generic training, we were told where we were to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't want to interfere with your examination of the witness. Do I understand your line of cross-examination to be suggesting that there is no distinction between UNPROFOR and UNMO? And I'm asking this question because the witness told us what his mandate was from the beginning of your cross-examination, which -- and his -- in his mandate, there was no reference whatsoever to peacekeeping. He has reiterated it right now without any reference to peacekeeping, and now, so far as I have understood, it seemed to me like that the job of peacekeeping was assigned to UNPROFOR rather than UNMOs. If you just sort of help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I'm happy to do that. Since you have asked for clarification on -- on two points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, is it your position that you as a member of an UNMO, United Nations Military Observer, were in a distinct organisation from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Distinct mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Distinct organisation. First of all is whether they're part of the same organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He answered to that. He said they had a different command structure. But if you want any further clarification on that, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were a separate organisation, if that's what you mean by distinct. There was one line -- one chain of command which was -- I was the team leader. I had one boss, which was the Senior Military Observer. He had another boss which was the Chief Military Observer in Zagreb. And, of course, there were links with UNPROFOR, because you both were working for UN, but we had a separate line of command which meant that my report went only to my Senior Military Observer who reported straight to the chief military observer, who reported straight to the UN council in New York, as far as I recollect. And of course, in a military operation you try to cooperates and share information on various levels. It would be stupid not to do that. But we were and I would classify it UNMOs are meant to be an independent, impartial organisation and can operate even without a military force being present. For that reason, they are independent. For that reason, we were not relying on logistics or whatever from other troops. So I had no contacts with UNPROFOR troops in the formal way.
