The only thing that we did is try to cooperate as well as we could with other UNPROFOR units inside Sarajevo, in order to, first of all, to -- to share information on the level that we were allowed by our Senior Military Observer, and, a very practical thing, in order to find some protection on some moments in time when it was quite dangerous to move around inside the city of Sarajevo because as you might recall, military observers have no weapons, they are on their own, and we had been threatened a lot inside the city of Sarajevo. So for that reason we had contacts with some of the battalions of UNPROFOR inside Sarajevo to be protected on certain moments during my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of your mandate, is it your testimony that the mandate of the UNMOs was distinct from the mandate of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I -- I can -- I cannot answer that question because I cannot recall exactly anymore the mandate of UNPROFOR in that period. I only know that we had the order to observe all the aspects that I already explained. I cannot make a comparison anymore. It's 15 years ago. I don't recall that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. One of the things you that have told us is that it was important for you to be impartial. Before you arrived in Sarajevo, were you briefed on any of the concerns that had been voiced by the Bosnian Serb army or by the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army with regard to issues that could affect impartially? And by that mean, their view of you being not impartial?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Of course, that fact was quite known in -- in any country that took part in UNPROFOR or delivered UNMOs to the conflict on the Balkan. Sorry. And I'm convinced that we were told about that in our training, because our training went into that kind of detail, that we had to expect different opinions about UNMOs, either being impartial or not. The conflict was ongoing already for several years, so the -- I was familiar with the fact that UNMOs were looked upon not being impartial or that UNPROFOR was looked upon as one of the parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that UNPROFOR was looked on -- was looked upon as one of the parties in the conflict, were you given specific examples of those assertions or allegations being made before you came to Sarajevo in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall any specific example, but as the public opinion was well aware of the role of UNPROFOR and the way UNPROFOR was looked upon in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But you can't remember any specific examples --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I cannot refer any specific example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to your statement that you were familiar with the fact that UNMOs were looked upon not being impartial, can you give us any further information, before you went, as to what you were told in that regard? What kind of things you were going to have to guard against or what kind of things you were going to have to convince the parties of in order establish your impartiality?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, in a generic sense, we were told to -- to treat all the involved parties in the same manner. Which means that you do not favour any party, that you are working with, or that you -- that you look upon the whole situation and try to see it from both sides, and that you just mere state the facts that you see. The best point to reach impartiality is that you just state -- you observe and report the facts that you see as they are happening. You don't make your own analysis on that. The analysis is done by others. Just by stating those facts you reach a certain level of impartiality. The other things is that you have to treat all parties that are involved in the same manner, which means that you meet them in the same manner, in the same open way, that you listen to them, and that you do not make promises that you are not allowed to make, or that you give advantages to a certain party more than advantages that you give to another party. Those are all types of generic guidelines that we were given in trying to act impartial as an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you informed with regard to what I'm now going to call the general view of the international presence in Sarajevo during the conflict period that allegations had been made by Mladic that UNPROFOR was supplying military equipment to the Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: UNPROFOR or UN --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- or UNM --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that I got that information. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information that any UNMO assets were being accused of being used by the Bosnian Serb army for purposes of assisting the Presidency forces? Not whether it is true or not but whether any allegations were made?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know. No. No, I have not received any information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were in Sarajevo, were you communicating information that you received with regard to your observations by telegraph, radio, telephone, fax, and other forms of electronic transmission?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We used radio and telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of any of your conversations being intercepted by any of the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was very well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your conversations being intercepted by parties to the conflict, what measures, if any, did you engage in, in your capacity to protect against the interception itself?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, we had very limited means. The only thing we could do is not use telephone or radio at all, and work with written reports that were brought as quickly as we could to the UNMO HQ. And in sensitive incidents, and most of them were sensitive, we tried to solve the problem as I described before. Another thing that we did is that when we had to use the radios, we made our own, well, secrecy system in giving grids. We never used the grid system that I described to you before. We had our own UNMO grid system that we changed by the day in order to avoid that any of the listening parties, Bosnian Serb or BiH, could get the information that we were sending. But especially later during the conflict, after July, we -- we refrained from using radios. If we could refrain that, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your tenure in Sarajevo, did you receive any information that your particular communications had been intercepted and had been used by either of the conflicting parties?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have had no specific feedback on that. But I -- I know that -- no, I don't know that. I cannot prove that. But I'm convinced that the information was used by both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of rumours, would it be fair to say, first generally, that in your capacity as a military observer, the issue of rumours was something that you had to guard against?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You received information with regard to rumours that the BiH snipers were targeting their own people. I'm not suggesting that they were true, I'm not suggesting that they were false. I'm just saying you received such rumour, did you not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, so ... I try to memorise that, but I really don't know anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive rumours concerning the issue of the planting or moving of bodies by either the BiH or Bosnian Muslims in order to stage an event, or to increase its apparent gravity? Once again, I'm only talking about the rumours; I'm not talking about the truth of the information.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We had specific guidelines from the Senior Military Observer during one of our team leader meetings that we had to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what were those guidelines?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Those guidelines were that we had to check, as far as we could, bodies that we were investigating in the morgue and try to establish an opinion about the status of the people that there were, the killed people, and try to find out whether they were -- well, I hate to use it, whether they were fresh killed people or that they were dragged around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that they were fresh killed people, they were dragged around, are you putting a time-frame on that, in terms of fresh killed people or dragged around?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, that has to do, of course, with the time-frame because that might be the difference that you -- when people are dragged around, that -- that means that they are dead for a longer period, several hours maybe, I don't know. But that's the only issue, the only guideline that the Senior Military Observer could give us knowing that we were -- neither of us was a medical expert or neither of us was a doctor. We only had to work with the experience that we had in our teams and maybe some personal experience that you have in looking to dead people, but after six months in Sarajevo you have some experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to issue of time of death and length of time between death and your examination, you've told us you're not a medical expert, I take it you received no training with regard to that issue?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We received no training to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You, as you sit here today, cannot give us information with regard to the various factors that go into the physiologic changes that occur to a body after it has ceased living, can you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: There are a few things we take into account. This were the stiffness of the body, whether blood was still coming out of wounds, very small issues that we tried to look upon than was the only thing that we could do because the time that was given us in the morgues to walk around and to check people was merely enough to count the people and to have a generic overview of -- of how many people there were, and how the situation was. We were not allowed by the Bosnian police to stay longer as necessary in the morgues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue that you just mentioned, being the stiffness of the body, I take it what you're referring to is the issue of rigor --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- that occurs in a body at some period of time after death. Do you know what the period is that a rigor is onset?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of blood still coming out of the wounds, can you tell us what training you received with regard to post-mortem blood flow?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We had no -- as I said before, we had no special training. We tried to -- to do -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking what -- what you did generic -- I'm asking what you did specifically. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I had no -- I had no training in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to issue of rumours concerning planting or moving of bodies, are you aware of the fact that this was a concern that was discussed not only in UNMO but also in UNPROFOR with people as high as General Nicolai and General Rupert Smith?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have heard that fact afterwards in the preparation of the General Milosevic case. I did not know that in that time because I had nothing to do with General Nicolai or General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Were you aware that, during the time that you were in Sarajevo, that before you came UNPROFOR had in the region heavy weapons in the nature of Leopard tanks?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I was aware of that fact. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that UNPROFOR had engaged in an operation in 1994, before you came, called Operation Bollebank in Tuzla in which they used heavy tanks?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific name of the operation and whether it was in Tuzla or not, but I know about the use of tanks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. While you were in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D00-7912 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would object to the use of this exhibit and, frankly, any exhibit by Defence counsel. We have yet to receive any notification of any exhibits to be used during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me double-check. At 10.56 a.m., a list was sent to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 10.56, what day, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can we please have identification of who specifically that e-mail was sent to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was sent to Carmela Javier, Viktorija Taseva, subject cross-examination, Konings. And it starts off: "Dear Carmela, the Defence for Mr. Perisic reserves the right to cross-examine Mr. Konings on any of the documents disclosed by the Prosecution in relation to his testimony, all of his prior testimony in those cases he has testified in at the Tribunal, in addition, all documents provided in the e-court system today." And then after that it says, "Potential exhibits," and there is a list that follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, I know -- Prosecution has not received that. I'm not certain about Ms. Taseva.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly request that counsel speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm looking at a message here that says 41 minutes ago. I'm more than happy to have it sent again. It has been our practice to send them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asked to speak into the microphone, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm more than happy to send it again. I don't know why it has not been received. We have an indication that it was sent. I can't take it any further because I'm not an electronic expert. I'm more than happy to have it sent again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would be at minimum. If we could also have that somehow written down in the event that we have another electronic issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Two seconds, so that I can take care of the administrative issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no desire whatsoever to put Ms. Carter at a disadvantage by not having those exhibits that we intend on using. I'm happy to take two minutes here to see whether it comes through in electronic transmission. We've sent someone out to get a hard copy. And I'm also happy to proceed. Whatever the Court wishes me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's going to depend on what Ms. Carter's objection's fate is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, it has just been sent again. And it has also been released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Send it also to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I guess this is the usual labour of the Defence, which is our systems don't work all that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, may I have the document that is being gestured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be much longer, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My apologies, I didn't realise that you were still waiting on me. If I can just have an extended break, I know that we're coming up soon. I will deal with the first exhibit but if it -- once we have a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I do want to find out from you, Madam Carter, is what you want to do with your objection now that that you have received the documents, and apparently they were sent at 10.56 this morning electronically. They were sent a couple of minutes ago electronically, and now you have them in hard copy. What do you want to do with your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, given it appears that Defence counsel have made their best efforts to get them timely, then I would withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Sarajevo, did you have occasion to see the kind of tank that is presently being shown on the screen, as 1D00-7912?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Were you aware of whether or not such a tank was in the region? Independently of having seen it, were you given any information with regard to such a tank being in the region?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Can you specify "region"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that the Leopard 1 was -- was in the armed forces of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the tank that you see before you is that a Leopard 1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is a Leopard 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what is the capability of a Leopard 1 with regard to the kind of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The Leopard 1 is not an artillery asset. The Leopard 1 is a direct fire platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you for the correction. And what is a direct fire platform?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This is a, as we call it in NATO terms, a main battle tank which is used for its fire-power, its flexibility, its manoeuvrability, and combined with infantry troops it can be used to conquer terrain, to perform an attack, to perform a defence. For that it has a -- it's a lethal -- a very lethal instrument with a 105-millimetre gun in it, heavy armour. It's quite fast, 60 kilometres on the road, so it's a real fighting machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have that moved in as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1D00-7912 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D78, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have P647 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you may be well familiar with this map, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at this map, with the assistance of the usher, would you be able to identify the confrontation lines that you were aware of during your tenure in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In all honesty, I cannot draw an exact line of the confrontation line anymore. We had that information on that time. It changed every day, so I really -- I'm not able to draw an exact line around Sarajevo where the confrontation line was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the confrontation line, are you in a position to give us an approximation of where the confrontation line was, using the grid system that you have explained to us during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I only are able to draw a rough line on a -- on a map that recollects or that gives you the area that I was responsible for, not around the whole Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the area that you were responsible for, can you, looking at this map, identify the area that you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I can give a rough estimation of the area that I was responsible for, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you please do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the area that you were responsible for, were you aware of any BiH troops being present in that area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In that area, there were some command posts located with some soldiers present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please mark where those command posts were located?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I'm not able to give you any precise location anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many command posts were located in the area that you have -- that you have designated you were responsible for by the drawing of the red box?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: To my recollection, I have been at at least four or five different command posts. One of them was located in one of the main streets inside the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say one of them was located one of the main streets inside of the city of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark on the outside of that box RA, for responsible area.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's a failure of English and Dutch. I believe it's A, not E.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's okay. Now, during the time that you were in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have that admitted as the defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D79, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D00-8658 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This would be identified, I believe, as D118 in the -- as the former Milosevic number, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive information that a gentleman by the name of Brigadier Prevljak discussed the firing of weapons between 15th of June and the 3rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document or information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have not seen this document?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm the information that is contained in this document is information that would comport with observations that UNMOs made, not your specific UNMO, but UNMOs made, who were in Sarajevo during the period of 15 June to July 3, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no detailed recollection of having heard or seen this information. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going to the second -- going to the second page. Does -- do you recognise the information is information that comes from the -- what we would call the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't recognise the document, so I'm not able to say anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact during the time that you were in Sarajevo that Brigadier Fikret Prevljak was a member of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Guy-Smith. There is a persistent noise in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm hearing the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- over here, so I'm not sure whether people who are typing or doing something, I would ask that we stop, please, except for the stenographer, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm hearing a low-level hum. I don't know if you're referring to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm continuously hearing some -- I don't know whether it's a low-level hum, but there's a lot of hum which suggests somebody's doing something. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can take this -- well, if you have no information about it, then we can go no further with regard to this document at this time. In your briefings, did you receive information about who were the commanders and active members of the BiH army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I am convinced that we got that information and, in fact, I met several battalion commanders of the BiH inside my area of operations. But I'm not able to recall any name anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is the information that you were just -- you were just looking at, the kind of information that would be important to you in terms of making an analysis and an assessment of what was occurring during the period of 15 June to 3 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, not specifically to me. As I told before, we were not there to analyse the situation. The analysis of anything that happened in and around Sarajevo was, first of all, a responsibility for, I think, for UNPROFOR itself. Any information that was given by the UNMOs was analysed in the HQ -- the respective HQs that I described. The thing that I was doing, my team was doing, was observing and stating the facts that we saw, and all these things that you showed me did not occur in the area that I was responsible for. So with the minimum -- with the limited resources that we have, and with limited resources, I mean personnel and materiel, we tried to see, to observe all the aspects, the incidents that were occurring in our area, and our main priority was concentrating on reporting on sniper and shelling incidents, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you and perhaps I was mistaken, but I thought that UNMOs independently collected and analysed information and reported directly to New York. That was -- part of the mandate of UNMO was in fact the collection as well as analysis of information. Am I incorrect in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, the UNMO organisation itself might do some analysis but teams on the ground, as my team did, we were the lowest part of the UNMO organisation, we did not make an analysis of the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. As a collector of information, you would understand, of course, the importance of collecting information so that people who were superior to you could analyse that information to make informed decisions how best to proceed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct but then you need to -- you only can inform the superiors about those things that you actually saw, that you actually observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. My question to you was: Whether or not the kind of information that is contained in that document, which is an assertion of multiple firings by the ABiH within Sarajevo from the discrete period of time of the -- of June through July, would be information that was important.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Of course, that's information that's important --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have P647 back up on the screen. You know what? Considering the time, why don't we start with P647 because that's going to come up on the screen, and by the time I ask the first question I think it will be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have P647 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, I'm going to ask you a question which is: In your capacity working as an UNMO, were you made aware of the demilitarised zone and the total exclusion zone that existed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such a zone, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I mentioned two different kinds. One was a demilitarised zone and the other was a total exclusion zone. I take it that you're not aware of either of those zones?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very good. With regard to the map that is up on the screen, looking at that map, can you identify the area where Sharpstone is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could mark that with an X?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I would appreciate if I would have a--

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A little bit bigger?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: A bit bigger outcut of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Before we start making anything bigger, is there any particular part of the map that you would like bigger, if would you divide it into quarters?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to have that part that I marked earlier on as the areas of operations of the team because that is the area that I'm rather familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we could then have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going need some help from Madam Registrar, if I could. It's -- I was going say D next in order, but that's going to be no help to you. D79? D79 up on the screen, please. Thank you very much. Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, would you like to -- I think we can have this area expanded. Would you like to have the area where you have --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate to have that area on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Sure. You want it a little bit bigger?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, I think then the view will be blurred even more than it is now, so it is very unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at that view, can you identify where Sharpstone is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I give you a very rough drawing, because the grids of Sharpstone are mentioned in various reports, but it is north -- here is the word Sedrenik mentioned which is the area where my team base was located. Sharpstone is about in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And could you mark that with an S.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And with regard to the area where Sharpstone has been indicated, and I understand that it is rough, was the Sharpstone area an area where there was a confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in the vicinity of Sharpstone there was a confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Using the same marker, I think we can go into the colour of blue, could you give us a rough idea of where the confrontation line was with relation to the Sharpstone area that you have marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Given the fact that the marking of Sharpstone here is very -- a rough identification of Sharpstone, it's not precise in the way I would like to see it as a military, but I'm quite sure that somewhere here was running part of the confrontation line, and the Serb army occupied this -- the front part of Sharpstone. How the confrontation line run further, I don't know. And how it run here in the forests, I'm also not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say here in the forest, could you mark with an F where there would be forests?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On the right-hand side seen from our team base, so in the east part of Sharpstone, in this area there were forests visible from my team base, which is an F.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And with regard to the area in between the edge of the box which is your area of responsibility going up towards Sharpstone, in that hiatus, is that an area that was occupied by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word occupied because I never have seen any BiH troops, with the exception of the fact that some -- during the night we had an exchange of troops that came from the confrontation line and passed our house and -- but there were no visible signs of areas that were occupied by troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Would it be fair to say that between where the hiatus -- what I'm calling a hiatus is, is an area that was under the control of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The area between Sedrenik and Sharpstone you might use the word control of the BiH, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please designate that area by inserting the letters BiH.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have that admitted as the Defence next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D80, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked some questions concerning P67, which is a report of the G2, and you explained to us what G2 was. And you were asked the following question on page 32: "You indicated that final conclusions were made than was actually made in an UNPROFOR G2 report as P67 in this case. Is that correct?" And your answer is: "That's one report where a conclusions were made, yes." My understanding is that you were unfamiliar with that report; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: At the time that -- when I was UNMO I was unfamiliar with that report. But that report has been shown to me in the preparation of the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have a proofing session with the Prosecution concerning testimony before you came to testify here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your testimony here, on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I had a session with the Prosecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you indicate to the Prosecution that you had no opinion of report P67 as you were not familiar with it, referring to paragraph 17 of the proofing notes that I received. Did you make that statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: If I made that statement then I probably have made that statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, if we also look at paragraph 23 he does make comments in relation to P67.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can deal with that in redirect if you wish I'm going to ask him a specific question regarding the information that he received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I would ask that the witness at least be allowed to look at the document that he is being basically impeached upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. If I can, I will give the witness a -- my copy. If I could just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could just take a quick look at -- Oh, here we go. Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost. What is the witness being impeached upon? The document on the screen or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. He's being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- on the proofing note?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we all see the proofing note, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't have the proofing note up on the screen because I received it at the last minute and was not able to upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will read to you what it says. Paragraph 17 reads: "Colonel Konings has no opinion of the report P67 as he is not familiar with it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, since we are -- in fairness to the witness I would also ask, since we're reading it into the record, page 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would appreciate if I would be allowed --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- paragraph 23, so as not to leave an incorrect description before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would appreciate if I would be allowed to ask my questions in a fashion that will fully examine the entire issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you make that statement to the Prosecutor, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I made this statement yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 23, it says: "The G2 report, P67, was drawn up with full intelligence. The G2 gathered all evidence and composed a report which would be given to the commander which in this case was Rupert Smith, commander of UNPROFOR." Did you make that statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you used the language "full intelligence," were you referring to what was done by UNPROFOR alone, or what was done by UNPROFOR and other organisations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I made that statement as to explain also to the Prosecution that a G2 uses all intelligence that he can receive or can use in order to build such a report, and this report, as far as I could judge about that, is that it used also the UNMO information. I'm not quite aware that other information from other organisations was used but it is quite clear that the G2 UNPROFOR report written for General Smith that the UNMO information was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your statement that you have no opinion of the report because you were not familiar with it, I take it that the statement that you just made to us here is something that you determined after you spoke with Ms. Carter concerning P67; is that correct? Since you were not familiar with the report prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I stated before, some moments ago, is that I have seen this report before and so I made a mistake yesterday in the Prosecution in stating that I have not seen this report before because the report was shown to me in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: So I'm sorry I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, mistakes are made. With regard to the conclusions that are contained in the G2 report, are you in agreement or disagreement with those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Could I see the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see any conclusions from the report. I only see the first page, the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This page states facts, so I just can agree -- I only can agree with the facts that are stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the summary, which are the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I can agree with that summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: With the exception -- with the exception of the fact that it states here that all impacts were from the same weapon or part of the same salvo. In my investigation I came to a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the conclusion that you came to is that there were different points of origin, correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So to the extent that this report indicates that the point of origin of all shells were from the same point, you disagree. True?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Looking to the facts that I saw on the -- on the spot, I disagree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. During the time that you were in Sarajevo and you were investigating shelling incidents, to your knowledge, were any members or authorities from Belgrade invited to come investigate the shellings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any members of the Bosnian Serb army invited to come investigate the shellings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no information about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any police personnel from Belgrade, experts in the area of shelling, invited to come investigate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the Bosnian Serb civil authorities in the Republika Srpska, are you aware of any individuals, such as police personnel, being invited to come and investigate the shellings that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no information about that at all. I haven't seen any personnel in my vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If could you to me a favour, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have P2292 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, this document which is coming up on the screen is the UNMO patrol report that was created on the 28th; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would have been at 1900 hours. True?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The report is written at 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a report that you personally penned; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The biggest part of the report is written by myself, with the exception of the cover remarks and the first sentence of the general part which was written by Flight Lieutenant Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The report before it was filed was reviewed by you and signed by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have reviewed the whole report, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- I believe it's the very last section of the report on the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's a section which I -- says PTLLDR's remarks. Does that stand for patrol leader's remarks?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And under patrol leader's remarks there are three separate items ; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The -- these are your remarks; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They are written by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And these are remarks that were written on 28th at the time that you compiled this report, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They were written shortly before the time that is in the top of the report, yes, somewhere between 1800 and 1900 hours that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you please read for us, because I'm having difficulty reading it, point number 3?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Can it be made -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That remark reads: "The investigation team tried very hard to prove that the attack came from the Serb side. Due to the normal use of heavy mortars that is likely but there is no hard proof on that fact."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As a follow-up to that remark, did you learn anything further or did your opinion change in regards to who was responsible for that kill shot?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, there were more facts coming in later that evening and the day afterwards, which gave extra evidence to underline the remark that due to the normal use of heavy mortars that is likely. Especially the evidence that came from OP-1, from the both observers that were working there, which I was able to speak on the 28th on the radio, but due to the limitations that we had with radios, I preferred to speak to them in a private session on the day after. That made the whole picture complete, when they stated that there were no outgoing rounds from their vicinity, which brought me to the conclusion that the round came from the Serb side. So, after the 29th, my personal opinion, which was actually of no interest on that moment, because I have to state the facts, and the facts were there was round fallen in the Markale. We had a found a bearing, we had found evidence of shrapnels and the tail, and we had the fact that there were outgoing rounds from the vicinity of OP-1. Well, then, that were the facts and that were the facts that we stated. So the conclusion that the round came from the Serb side was made by UNPROFOR, by General Rupert Smith, not by the UNMOs, not by me at least. But my personal opinion on the 29th was that the round came from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I have a question for you. I'd like to know precisely where the mortar came from? Did it come from the south or the north of Sarajevo, in your view?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As we designated the bearing to be 100 -- as we designated the bearing, the direction to be 170 degrees, which means that practically due south from the city. It came from the southern direction from the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So am I to understand that it came from the area where OP-1 was, from the same direction, that is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one point I would like to raise with you, sir. You told us that you used to have meetings of the UNMO leaders from both the Serb side and the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Then I did -- did -- then I did not express myself maybe very clear. We had team leader meetings with the team leaders on a regular basis from only -- that were working on the Bosnian BiH side. Because the team leaders that were working on the Serb side were in, I think, 90 per cent of the cases that we had a meeting were not allowed to cross the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in fact you even said that in such situations there would telephonic contact with them.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Then our Senior Military Observer, or one of his staff officers, they would have telephone contact with them. I never had reason to have a telephone contact with team leaders at the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the idea had been to have these meetings because it couldn't happen because they were not allowed to cross.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Of course. Because having a combined team leader meetings with all the teams of the sector of Sarajevo, that is a very, very important thing to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now at least in 10 percent of the time you did have these meetings.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about the figure but once or twice I met one of the team leaders that were able to cross the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me make myself clear: I'm not asking about you personally meeting the team leaders. I'm talking about a meeting of the team leaders from the Serb side and from the Serbs -- Bosnian side, where you exchanged notes. When I say "you," I mean UNMOs, UNMO leadership. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I can only judge about the time that I was there. As far as I can recall, it only happened once, maybe twice, that one or two team leaders from the Serb side were available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Were you personally privy, to -- let me not use the word "privy." Did you have access to the minutes of their meetings of the leaders, as and when they did happen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I even do not recall whether there were specific written minutes of those meetings. I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you have any access to any information that was exchanged between them?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Of course, most of the time I was present myself, and when I was not present my deputy team leader was present and then we could share that information orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were present yourself in the meetings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's confine ourselves to those meetings were you were present and some leaders from the Republika Srpska were present. In those meetings, do you have any recollection on whether any exchange of information was given to you by the leaders from the Republika Srpska concerning incidents of this nature, like the Markale incidents, that may have taken place on their side?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Never had --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not about -- there were no reports about incidents in the same -- parallel to what happened on Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But incidents of any --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Of course there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- shelling or sniping by the -- any attack?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They were, of course, reports about fire exchanges, because that happened. There were fire exchanges around the confrontation line between Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian army troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they exchange information with you about incidents which they investigated?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They did investigations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: But they were very restricted, that was what I recall. They had not the opportunities that we had on the Bosnian army side to go there together with police forces. They most times were restricted to their houses and had hardly any freedom of movement. That's very something -- something that is very clear to me from that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- how did they then conduct the investigations if they were restricted to their houses?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It means that they only on a very occasions were allowed to get out of their house to do an investigation. So most of the incidents that occurred were not investigated by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Let's confine ourselves to the few incidents that they did investigate. Did you -- did they report to you -- when I say "report," exchange information on any such investigations which they did indeed investigate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, they filed, of course, towards the Senior Military Observer their patrol reports and their incidents reports, as have you seen in the way that I did. And there were no specific detailed discussions during the team leader meetings on highlighting one of those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In your exchange of information, are you aware whether when they did go out for investigations they were accompanied by any representatives of the Republika Srpska, either the army or authorities of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I think they were controlled -- they were -- they were in -- they were only allowed to do that in very close cooperation with Serb authorities, either police or army. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the exchange of information with you did they mention whether BiH authorities had been invited?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. I don't think they mentioned that. I'm not quite sure but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether indeed BiH authorities were invited?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Madam Carter, any questions arising from the questions by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you so much for taking time off from your busy schedule to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Three points. First of all, may Ms. Carter please be excused so that she may bid farewell to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, do you want to bid farewell to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time and that normally we would continue for another 40 minutes today. It is my understanding that the next witness, Mr. Starcevic, at this time is in the middle of a proofing session with Mr. Harmon, and the Prosecution would seek leave to call Mr. Starcevic beginning at 9.00 tomorrow morning with the leave of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually, the Prosecution is asking for an adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Effectively right, yes, Your Honour. Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, except that I also have a procedural matter, Your Honour, that I wanted to raise with you. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has received a courtesy copy of a decision that I believe will be filed forthwith by the Chamber granting a recent Prosecution motion to lead evidence via videolink technology for three witnesses from Sarajevo. Your Honour, the decision of the Trial Chamber consistent with the motion sets the date for that videolink testimony as the 5th of May. And the Prosecution would respectfully ask that the videolink testimony actually be moved up to this coming Monday, the 27th of April, because we believe that that day will actually be vacant at this time, and so we would respectfully request a modification of your videolink decision, bringing the date forward to Monday, the 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so modified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. That's all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That brings us to the end of the session for the day. Court stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I. Just a second, Judge. Indeed, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
